entry:
Arab religious, military, and political leader, founder of [[Islam]]. According to Islam, he was the final prophet of God, divinely inspired to preach and confirm the monotheistic teachings of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and other prophets. Muslims believe him to be the Seal of the Prophets, and his teachings and normative examples, along with the [[Quran]], form the basis of Islamic religious belief.

According to the traditional account, he was born in [[Mecca]] to the aristocratic Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh and was orphaned at the age of six, raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and his uncle Abu Talib. In c. 610, at age 40, he reported being visited by [[Gabriel]] in the cave of Hira and receiving his first revelation. From 613 he preached publicly that "God is One" and that complete "submission" (*Islām*) to God is the right way of life. His followers, initially few, were persecuted by Meccan polytheists for 13 years. In 622 they migrated to [[Medina]] (then Yathrib), an event, the Hijrah, that marks the beginning of the [[Islamic calendar]]. There he united the tribes under the Constitution of Medina. In December 629, after eight years of intermittent fighting with Meccan tribes, he marched on Mecca with an army of 10,000 converts and seized it with minimal casualties. He died in 632, a few months after the Farewell Pilgrimage; by then most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam.

The revelations he reported form the verses of the Quran, which Muslims regard as the verbatim word of God. His teachings and practices, recorded in transmitted reports known as [[Hadith|hadith]] and in his biography (*sīrah*), are also sources of Islamic law. The earliest surviving biographies date from the 8th and 9th centuries, and their reliability is contentious in academic circles. He also holds a significant role in the [[Druze]] faith as one of seven main prophets, and in the Baháʼí Faith as a Manifestation of God.

City (pop., 2011: almost 12.5 million), capital of [[Maharashtra]] state and financial capital of India, on the Konkan coast. Also known as Bombay, it has a deep natural harbour and is the most populous city proper in India; the Mumbai Metropolitan Region has over 20 million people. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, established in 1888, administers the city.

Originally an archipelago of seven islands on the [[Arabian Sea]], it has evidence of human occupation from the South Asian Stone Age. The [[Maurya Empire]] ruled the islands from the 3rd century BC, and Ptolemy referred to them in AD 150. They were inhabited by the Marathi-speaking Koli people, whose deity Mumbā is believed to have given the city its name. Later rulers included the Satavahanas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, and Shilaharas, followed by the [[Delhi Sultanate]] and the Gujarat Sultanate. The islands were ceded to the Portuguese in 1535, transferred to the British Crown in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry, and leased to the [[East India Company]] in 1668. The Hornby Vellard land-reclamation project, begun in 1782 and completed in 1845, unified the islands; with new roads and railways and the 19th-century [[Cotton|cotton]] boom, it made Bombay a major seaport and commercial centre. The city played a major role in the [[Indian independence movement]] and became capital of Maharashtra in 1960.

The Government of India officially changed the English name to Mumbai in November 1995, at the insistence of the Shiv Sena party, which argued that "Bombay" echoed British colonial rule. Some residents still use the older name, and use of other names has become controversial. In the early 2010s the city contributed nearly five percent of India's GDP, one-fourth of its industrial output, and one-third of its tax revenues. It is the centre of Bollywood and Marathi cinema.

Japanese novelist, poet, and lady-in-waiting at the imperial court during the [[Heian period]]. She is best known as the author of *[[The Tale of Genji]]*, widely considered one of the world's first novels, written in Japanese between about 1000 and 1012. "Murasaki Shikibu" is a descriptive name; her personal name is unknown, though she may have been Fujiwara no Kaoruko, named in a 1007 court diary as a lady-in-waiting.

Heian women were traditionally excluded from learning Chinese, the written language of government, but Murasaki, raised in the household of her father, the scholar Fujiwara no Tametoki, showed a precocious aptitude for the Chinese classics and became fluent. She married in her mid-to-late twenties and had a daughter, Daini no Sanmi; her husband died after two years. She probably began *The Tale of Genji* while married or soon after being widowed. In about 1005 Fujiwara no Michinaga invited her to serve as lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi, probably because of her reputation as a writer, and she continued writing at court, adding scenes of court life. After five or six years she left court and retired with Shōshi to the Lake Biwa region. Scholars differ on the year of her death: most agree on 1014, while others suggest she was alive in 1025.

She wrote *The Diary of Lady Murasaki*, *The Tale of Genji*, and a volume of poetry. Within a decade of its completion, *Genji* was distributed throughout the provinces; within a century it was recognized as a classic of [[Japanese literature]] and had become a subject of scholarly criticism. It was published in English between 1925 and 1933. Her works reflect Heian court society at its peak, and since the 13th century they have been illustrated by Japanese artists, including well-known [[Ukiyo-e|ukiyo-e]] woodblock masters.

Specialized soft tissue, one of the four basic types of animal tissue, whose cells contract to produce force and movement. In vertebrates there are three types: [[Skeletal muscle|skeletal]], cardiac, and smooth muscle. All contain the contractile proteins actin and myosin, which interact to cause movement, along with the regulatory proteins troponin and tropomyosin. Muscle forms during embryonic development in a process called myogenesis.

Skeletal muscle is striated and made of elongated, multinucleate cells called muscle fibers, 10 to 100 micrometers wide, arranged in parallel bundles of myofibrils containing contractile units called [[Sarcomere|sarcomeres]]. Anchored to bone by [[Tendon|tendons]], it contracts voluntarily under the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] and moves the body and maintains posture. It makes up 42% of the body mass of an average adult man and 36% of an average adult woman. Cardiac muscle, found only in the walls of the [[Heart|heart]], is striated but involuntary, with branching fibers joined at intercalated discs. Smooth muscle, non-striated and involuntary, lies in the walls of organs and structures including the esophagus, stomach, intestines, uterus, bladder, and blood vessels.

Skeletal muscle fibers are classified as type I (slow-twitch), rich in capillaries, [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]], and myoglobin and suited to sustained aerobic activity, or type II (fast-twitch), which contracts more quickly and with greater force but sustains only short anaerobic bursts. Mammalian skeletal muscle has a density of about 1.06 kg/liter, roughly 15% denser than fat. Muscle types differ in their response to [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitters]] and hormones such as acetylcholine, adrenaline, and nitric oxide. In all types, contraction depends on calcium ions triggering interaction between actin and myosin filaments. Muscle also produces heat, as in shivering. The word derives from Latin *musculus*, a diminutive of *mus*, "mouse", because a flexed biceps resembles the back of a mouse.

Institution dedicated to displaying and preserving culturally or scientifically significant objects. Many museums exhibit their objects publicly, and some hold non-exhibited collections used by researchers and specialists. Collections often focus on a theme such as the arts, science, natural history, or local history, and the most visited museums draw millions of visitors annually.

The English word comes via Latin from the [[Ancient Greek]] *mouseion*, a place or temple dedicated to the [[Muses]], and hence a building set apart for study and the arts, especially the Musaeum at [[Alexandria]], built under [[Ptolemy I Soter]] about 280 BC. Museums originated as private collections of interesting items, and an emphasis on educating the public came much later. Modern public museums grew out of European "cabinets of curiosities," and the [[Louvre]] opened in 1793, after the [[French Revolution]], as a national public gallery. In the 19th century museums focused mainly on scientific research and the organization of collections, especially natural history specimens, and were mostly for scholars. In the latter half of the 20th century, reduced government funding pushed museums to rely on private support and to attract visitors with interactive exhibits. In the 21st century they emphasize accessibility and inclusion, use digital tools such as virtual tours and online collections, and host discussion of social issues.

The International Council of Museums' definition, adopted in 2022, describes a museum as a not-for-profit, permanent institution in the service of society that researches, collects, conserves, interprets, and exhibits tangible and intangible heritage. Approximately 95,000 museums operate worldwide, up from 22,000 in 1975. The American Alliance of Museums reports that U.S. museums contribute over 18 million instructional hours annually and $50 billion to GDP. The 2015 Recommendation of [[UNESCO]] stresses combating illicit trafficking and sustainable conservation. Debates persist over the ethical acquisition of objects in colonial eras and demands for their repatriation.

Art of arranging sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, or other expressive content. Music is generally agreed to be a cultural universal, present in all human societies, though definitions vary widely and scholars have reached no consensus on which elements are necessary. Its making is often divided into composition, improvisation, and performance. It may be performed on a wide variety of [[Musical instrument|musical instruments]], including the human voice, or produced mechanically or electronically, as by a music box, a barrel organ, or digital audio workstation software.

Music plays a key role in social events and religious ceremonies, and its techniques are often transmitted as part of a cultural tradition. It is performed in public and private settings, at festivals and concerts for various ensembles, and is used in the soundtracks of films, television shows, operas, and video games. Listening is a common means of entertainment, and the culture around music extends to academic study, journalism, philosophy, psychology, and therapy. The [[Music industry|music industry]] includes songwriters, composers, performers, sound engineers, producers, tour organizers, distributors of instruments, and publishers of sheet music and recordings. Recording and reproduction technology has included sheet music, microphones, phonographs, and tape machines, with digital playback common on MP3 players, CD players, and smartphones.

The word entered English in the 1630s, from Middle English *musike*, Old French *musique*, and Latin *mūsica*, ultimately from the Greek *mousiké technē*, "art of the [[Muses]]". Concepts of music vary across cultures. Before Western contact, neither Japan nor China had a single word covering music in a broad sense; the Chinese *yue* shares a character with *le*, "joy". The Songye of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Tiv of Nigeria have a broad conception of music but no corresponding word. The Hindi *sangita* properly refers to art music.

Origins are debated. Many scholars see a relationship with the [[Origin of language|origin of language]], and disagree on whether music arose before, after, or alongside it, and on whether it was a direct result of natural selection or a byproduct of evolution. [[Charles Darwin]] proposed in 1871 that music arose through sexual selection, perhaps via mating calls; the theory has been heavily criticized, though some 21st-century scholars have promoted it. Other theories hold that music arose to organize labor, aid long-distance communication, communicate with the divine, build community cohesion, or scare off predators. The disputed Divje Babe flute, a perforated cave bear femur, is at least 40,000 years old. The earliest widely accepted instruments are bone flutes from the Swabian Jura, Germany: eight examples, four made from bird wing bones and four from mammoth ivory, with three from Geissenklösterle dated oldest, c. 43,150–39,370 BP.

In [[Ancient Egypt]], harps, flutes, and double clarinets are securely attested in the Old Kingdom, and percussion instruments, lyres, and lutes joined orchestras by the Middle Kingdom. The "Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal", found on clay tablets in the Syrian city of [[Ugarit]] and dating to approximately 1400 BC, is the oldest surviving notated work of music. In ancient Greece music was one of the main subjects taught to children, with boys beginning at age six, and musical education was considered important for the development of the soul, as in [[Plato]]'s *Republic*. Instruments included the double-reed aulos and the lyre, especially the kind called a kithara.

Device created or adapted to make musical sounds. In principle any sound-producing object can be a musical instrument; purpose makes it one. A person who plays one is an instrumentalist. Early instruments may have served rituals, such as a horn to signal success on a hunt or a drum in a ceremony, before cultures developed melodies for entertainment.

The date and origin of the first instrument are widely disputed. The oldest object identified by scholars as an instrument is a simple [[Flute|flute]] dated 50,000–60,000 years ago, though many scholars date early flutes to about 40,000 years ago. Most early instruments were made of perishable materials such as animal skins, bone, and wood, so dating the first is considered impossible by many historians. The Divje Babe flute, a perforated bone found in 1995 in northwest [[Slovenia]] by Ivan Turk, is estimated at 43,400 to 67,000 years old; many argue that carnivores chewing the bone produced it, while Turk and others argue it is a [[Neanderthal]]-made flute. Mammoth bone and swan bone flutes of 30,000 to 37,000 years ago from the Swabian Alps of Germany are more commonly accepted as the oldest known instruments. Excavations at the Royal Cemetery in the Sumerian city of [[Ur]] also uncovered instruments.

Instruments developed independently in many regions, but contact among civilizations spread and adapted most of them. By the post-classical era, instruments from [[Mesopotamia]] were in maritime [[Southeast Asia]], and Europeans played instruments originating from North Africa. By 1400 development had slowed in many areas. Many new instruments appeared between roughly 1750 and 1900, and electricity led to new electric and electronic instruments such as the [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]], the [[Synthesizer|synthesizer]], and the theremin.

The most common academic classification, the Hornbostel–Sachs system, groups instruments by how they produce sound. Developed in 1914 by Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs, it divides them into idiophones, membranophones, chordophones, and aerophones; electrophones were added later. Western orchestral practice instead groups them as strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion. The academic study of instruments is called organology.

Country (pop., 2024: about 51 million) in northwest [[Southeast Asia]]; capital, Naypyidaw. Officially the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and also called Burma (the official English name until 1989), it is the largest country by area in Mainland Southeast Asia. Its largest city is [[Yangon]] (formerly Rangoon). It is bordered by India, Bangladesh, China, Laos, Thailand, the Andaman Sea, and the Bay of Bengal.

Early civilizations included the Tibeto-Burman-speaking [[Pyu city-states]] and the Mon kingdoms. The Bamar entered the upper Irrawaddy valley in the 9th century, and after the [[Pagan Kingdom]] was established in the 1050s, Burmese language and culture and Theravada Buddhism became dominant. Reunified by the Taungoo dynasty in the 16th century, the country briefly became the largest empire in Southeast Asian history. The [[Konbaung dynasty]] ruled in the early 19th century; after three Anglo-Burmese Wars, Britain made the country a colony. Independence came in 1948. A coup in 1962 brought military rule, and the military junta that followed the 1988 8888 Uprising governed directly until 2011. The National League for Democracy, led by [[Aung San Suu Kyi]], took power after the 2015 election, though the treatment of ethnic minorities, particularly the Rohingya, caused international tension. After the NLD won the 2020 election, the military again seized power in the 2021 coup, citing alleged electoral irregularities, which led to widespread protests and an ongoing [[Civil war|civil war]].

In 1989 the military government changed the English name from Burma to Myanmar. The change remains contested: opposition groups and some countries still use Burma, while the UN and [[ASEAN]] use Myanmar.

The country has resources including jade, gems, oil, natural gas, and teak, but suffers from political instability, corruption, poor infrastructure, and low human development, and is classified as one of the least developed countries. According to the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, over 1.3 million refugees and asylum seekers and over 3.5 million internally displaced people result from the conflict.

Death (infarction) of part of the heart muscle caused by decreased or stopped blood flow in a coronary artery; commonly called a heart attack. The most common symptom is retrosternal chest pain or discomfort that classically radiates to the left shoulder, arm, or jaw. Other symptoms include shortness of breath, nausea, feeling faint, a cold sweat, and fatigue. Women more often present without chest pain, instead having neck or arm pain or fatigue. Among those over 70–75, about 5% have had an infarction with little or no history of symptoms. It may cause [[Heart failure|heart failure]], an irregular heartbeat, cardiogenic shock, or [[Cardiac arrest|cardiac arrest]].

Most cases result from [[Coronary artery disease|coronary artery disease]]; the usual mechanism is complete blockage of a coronary [[Artery|artery]] by the rupture of an [[Atherosclerosis|atherosclerotic]] plaque. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, lack of exercise, obesity, high cholesterol, poor diet, and excessive alcohol intake. Less commonly, coronary artery spasms caused by cocaine, significant emotional stress (Takotsubo syndrome), or extreme cold are responsible.

Diagnosis uses [[Electrocardiography|electrocardiograms]], blood tests for troponin, and coronary angiography. An ECG distinguishes ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) from non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Treatment is time-critical. [[Aspirin]] is an appropriate immediate treatment; oxygen is recommended for low oxygen levels. In a STEMI, treatment aims to restore blood flow through percutaneous coronary intervention, in which arteries are opened and may be stented, or through thrombolysis with medications. NSTEMI is often managed with the blood thinner heparin, with percutaneous intervention for those at high risk. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be recommended for people with multiple blocked arteries and diabetes. After an infarction, lifestyle changes and long-term aspirin, beta blockers, and statins are typically recommended.

About 15.9 million myocardial infarctions occurred worldwide in 2015. STEMIs occur about twice as often in men as in women, and in the developed world the risk of death after a STEMI is about 10%. Age-specific rates decreased globally between 1990 and 2010.

Genre of [[Folklore|folklore]] consisting primarily of narratives that play a fundamental role in a society. For scholars this differs from the ordinary sense of the term, a belief that is not true: the veracity of a piece of folklore is irrelevant to whether it constitutes a myth.

Myths are often endorsed by religious and secular authorities and may be natural or supernatural in character. Many societies group their myths, legends, and history together as factual accounts of their remote past. [[Creation myth|Creation myths]] take place in a primordial age before the world achieved its later form, origin myths explain how a society's customs, institutions, and taboos were established and sanctified, and national myths symbolize a nation's values. The relationship between the recital of myths and the enactment of [[Ritual|rituals]] is complex.

Main characters are usually gods, demigods, and other supernatural figures; stories of ordinary humans are usually classed as [[Legend|legends]]. Myths are sometimes distinguished from legends in that they deal with gods, usually have no historical basis, and are set in a remote past very different from the present. Many exceptions and combinations exist, and as faiths change, myths may come to be considered folktales, with divine characters recast as giants, elves, or fairies. Definitions vary among scholars. The Finnish folklorist Lauri Honko describes a myth as a religious account of the world's beginning and the exemplary deeds of the gods, which expresses a society's religious values, provides patterns of behavior to imitate, and establishes the sanctity of cult. Some scholars in other fields use the word broadly for any traditional story, popular misconception, or imaginary entity.

The word comes from [[Ancient Greek]] *mythos*, meaning "speech", "narrative", or "fiction". [[Plato]] used *mythología* as a general term for fiction or story-telling of any kind. English adopted *mythology* in the 15th century, first attested in John Lydgate's *Troy Book* (c. 1425), and *myth* itself appeared only in 1830.
